hints: Recall the link between enthalpy of reaction and enthalpies of formation for products and reactants, paying attention to which terms are added and which are subtracted.
Check the balanced equation carefully to see how many moles of $\text{AgF}$ and $\text{AgI}$ must be included in the calculation.
Substitute all four $\Delta H_f$ values with correct signs and combine them to find $\Delta H_r$ in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Set up the Hess rule**
Think of formation enthalpies as building every compound from its elements. To get the reaction enthalpy you build the products up, then unbuild the reactants. That gives $$\Delta H_r = \Sigma \Delta H_f(\text{products}) - \Sigma \Delta H_f(\text{reactants})$$

Multiply by the balancing numbers**
Look at the equation: $$\text{CHI}_3(\text{s}) + 3\text{AgF}(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{CHF}_3(\text{g}) + 3\text{AgI}(\text{s})$$ One mole of $\text{CHF}_3$ and three moles of $\text{AgI}$ are formed, while one mole of $\text{CHI}_3$ and three moles of $\text{AgF}$ are used up. So you must multiply the $\text{AgI}$ and $\text{AgF}$ values by 3.

Substitute and calculate**
Put the numbers in with their signs: $$\Delta H_r = [(-692.9) + 3(-61.8)] - [(-182.1) + 3(-204.6)]$$ $$\Delta H_r = (-878.3) - (-795.9) = -82.4 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign shows the reaction is exothermic.

Final answer: $\Delta H_r = \Sigma \Delta H_f(\text{products}) - \Sigma \Delta H_f(\text{reactants})$
$= (-692.9) + 3(-61.8) - (-182.1) - 3(-204.6) = -82.4 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Picture an ideal gas as tiny dots flying around a huge empty box, then ask what this implies about their own size compared with the container.
Think about whether ideal particles are supposed to attract or repel each other when they are far apart.
Consider what happens to total kinetic energy when two ideal particles collide.
walkthrough:
Imagine the ideal particle**
Forget real molecules for a moment. Scientists model an ideal gas as point masses with mass but essentially zero size. They zoom around randomly in a container that is mostly empty space.

Remove attractions and repulsions**
In the ideal model there are no forces between particles except during the instant of collision. That is why a real polar molecule like $\text{CHF}_3$ is only approximately ideal at low pressure when particles are far apart.

Keep collisions perfect**
When ideal particles hit each other or the wall, the collisions are perfectly elastic, so no kinetic energy is lost. The gas also obeys all gas laws such as $pV = nRT$ exactly.

Final answer: 1. Molecules have negligible volume compared to volume of container.
2. No intermolecular forces between molecules.
3. Collisions between molecules are elastic.

hints: Use the graph to see that above about 300 atm the $pV$ for $\text{CHF}_3$ rises above the ideal line, then think about what high pressure does to the distance between molecules.
Recall which ideal gas assumption about particle size breaks down when particles are squeezed very close together.
walkthrough:
Read what the graph is telling you**
For an ideal gas $pV$ is constant, a flat dashed line. For $\text{CHF}_3$ above about 300 atm the curve climbs above that line, so the measured $pV$ is too large. Something is making the gas harder to compress than expected.

Squeeze the particles together**
High pressure means the same number of moles in a much smaller volume. The $\text{CHF}_3$ molecules are now so close that the empty space assumption fails. Their own volume is no longer negligible, and short range repulsive forces between electron clouds become important, giving a larger volume and larger $pV$ than ideal.

Final answer: At pressures greater than 300 atm molecules are forced very close together.
The volume of the molecules themselves becomes significant compared to the total volume / repulsive forces become significant, so $pV$ is greater than ideal.

hints: List all atoms on each side starting from $\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{COCl}_2 + \text{HCl}$ and see which elements are already balanced and which need adjusting.
walkthrough:
Balance by inspection**
Write the skeleton: $\text{CHCl}_3$ plus $\text{O}_2$ gives $\text{COCl}_2$ ($\text{C}$ double bonded to $\text{O}$) plus $\text{HCl}$. $\text{C}$, $\text{H}$ and $\text{Cl}$ already balance with one of each product. You need only one $\text{O}$ atom on the left, so use $\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$. That gives $$\text{CHCl}_3 + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{COCl}_2 + \text{HCl}$$

hints: Compare the structures of $\text{CHCl}_3$ and $\text{COCl}_2$ and spot which bond type is present in the product but completely absent in the starting material.
Recall the characteristic wavenumber range for that bond in the Data Booklet and find the matching strong sharp dip on the spectrum.
walkthrough:
Spot the new functional group**
$\text{CHCl}_3$ has only $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{C-Cl}$ bonds. Carbonyl dichloride, $\text{COCl}_2$, has a $\text{C=O}$ double bond. A bond that did not exist before must give a new absorption.

Locate the carbonyl peak**
The $\text{C=O}$ stretch gives a very strong, sharp absorption at 1670 to 1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. On the spectrum this is the deep dip to near zero transmittance at about 1700 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. Mark this with X, because $\text{CHCl}_3$ with no $\text{C=O}$ cannot absorb there.

Final answer: X marked on strong absorption at 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
This is the $\text{C=O}$ stretch, $\text{CHCl}_3$ contains no $\text{C=O}$ bond so this absorption would not be present in $\text{CHCl}_3$.

hints: Look for a bond containing hydrogen in $\text{CHCl}_3$ that is lost when $\text{COCl}_2$ and $\text{HCl}$ are formed.
walkthrough:
Find a peak that disappears**
$\text{CHCl}_3$ contains a $\text{C-H}$ bond, which absorbs at 2850 to 2950 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. Carbonyl dichloride, $\text{COCl}_2$, has no hydrogen at all, so its spectrum has no absorption in that region. The disappearance of the $\text{C-H}$ peak is another clear difference.
Final answer: $\text{CHCl}_3$ shows absorption at 2850-2950 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C-H}$ which is absent in $\text{COCl}_2$.
